summary: Amina Ali Qassim and her family escaped their home on Yemen's Birim island just before missiles destroyed it, then crossed to Djibouti the next morning. They joined three other families in a crowded boat carrying 25 people on a difficult five-hour journey across the Bab al-Mandab Strait. They are staying in an unfinished orphanage in Obock before moving to tents outside town, while the United Nations expects thousands more refugees. With nearly all their belongings gone, Qassim fears for her two daughters trapped in Taiz, whom she cannot reach, and for the lasting effect of the bombardment on her infant granddaughter.

Australian police arrested five men aged 18 or 19 Saturday in Melbourne over an alleged plan to attack police during the April 25 Anzac Day commemoration of the Gallipoli campaign's centennial. Three were released pending further investigation, while Sevdet Besim, 18, was charged with conspiring to commit a terrorist act and denied bail. A second detainee, 19, had not yet appeared in court. Investigators said evidence suggested ISIS had inspired the alleged plot and warned of a risk to the public, but police said the specific threat was fully contained. Police said the suspects were associates of Nadun Haider, 18, who was killed in September while stabbing officers. They emphasized that the men did not represent any religious, cultural or national group and urged broader community efforts to identify young people becoming involved in extremism. Prime Minister Tony Abbott cited earlier extremist incidents and said about 100 Australians were fighting alongside terrorists in the Middle East, with another 150 in Australia providing financial or recruitment support. His government had announced stricter citizenship laws as part of its counterterrorism strategy, and authorities had suspended passports of people suspected of terrorist activity. Abbott encouraged Australians to continue their normal lives and attend Anzac Day events in large numbers.

Hundreds of decomposed corpses were discovered buried in shallow graves in the streets of the northeastern Nigerian town of Damasak this past weekend, according to local officials and a resident. The victims included men, women and children murdered by Boko Haram when they seized the area in November, said Abubakar Kyari, a senator-elect for the region.

ISIS claimed responsibility for a suicide car bomb attack Friday near the U.S. Consulate in the Kurdish Iraqi city of Irbil, according to several Twitter accounts linked to the terror group. At least four people were killed and 18 injured, police said, while Peshmerga spokesman Hazhar Ismail said three civilians were killed and five others were injured. Security personnel fired at the car, which exploded but did not reach the consulate, a police official said. All U.S. Consulate personnel were safe and accounted for following the explosion, U.S. State Department spokeswoman Marie Harf said.

James Best, best known for his portrayal of bumbling sheriff Rosco P. Coltrane on TV's "The Dukes of Hazzard," died Monday after a brief illness at 88. Best died in hospice in Hickory, North Carolina, of complications from pneumonia, said Steve Latshaw, a longtime friend and Hollywood colleague. Although he'd been a busy actor for decades in theater and in Hollywood, Best didn't become famous until 1979, when "The Dukes of Hazzard's" cornpone charms began beaming into millions of American homes almost every Friday night. For seven seasons, Best's Rosco P. Coltrane chased the moonshine-running Duke boys back and forth across the back roads of fictitious Hazzard County, Georgia, although his "hot pursuit" usually ended with him crashing his patrol car. Among the most popular shows on TV in the early '80s, "The Dukes of Hazzard" ran until 1985 and spawned TV movies, an animated series and video games. Several of Best's "Hazzard" co-stars paid tribute to the late actor on social media. Born Jewel Guy on July 26, 1926, in Powderly, Kentucky, Best was orphaned at 3 and adopted by Armen and Essa Best, who renamed him James and raised him in rural Indiana. Best served in the Army during World War II before launching his acting career. In the 1950s and 1960s, he accumulated scores of credits, playing a range of colorful supporting characters in such TV shows as "The Twilight Zone," "Bonanza," "The Andy Griffith Show" and "Gunsmoke."

Feidin Santana said an officer ordered him to stop filming the fatal shooting of unarmed Walter Scott by North Charleston officer Michael Slager, and fear for his safety nearly kept him from releasing the video. The recording showed Slager firing at Scott as he fled and led to Slager's dismissal and arrest on a murder charge, while accounts conflicted over whether Scott received CPR.

The latest high-profile digital incursion, in December, attempted to steal data from South Korea's nuclear operator, including plant blueprints and personnel information. Codes used in the attack were said to be similar in pattern to those used by the North Koreans, South Korean authorities said.

Koch Industries' recent announcement that it will "ban the box" -- i.e., remove from its job applications the check-box that asks about convictions -- is a big step forward in the movement to break down barriers to employment for job-seekers with records. "Ban the box" doesn't prohibit background checks, it only postpones them until later in the hiring process. So far, 16 states and more than 100 cities and counties have adopted fair-chance hiring policies. Now it's time for President Obama to lead the way and embrace fair-chance hiring of people with records.

The migrant crisis that has suddenly drawn hundreds of journalists to Sicily has been brewing for years, but in the past 10 days, with as many as 1,600 deaths in the Mediterranean, suddenly minds are focused -- for now. The fall of Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi's regime, which we reporters covered so avidly, was followed by chaos, which we in the news media largely neglected, focused as we journalists were on the next catastrophe, the Syrian civil war. In that chaos, the business of human trafficking has boomed. Aware of the tragedy underway, however, Italians are alarmed at the prospect that this year alone as many as a million migrants could arrive in Europe, according to one European Union official. The city's mayor, Enzo Bianco, insists city residents bear no ill will toward the migrants, but says Catania, and Sicily cannot absorb the ever-growing numbers. The rest of Europe must help carry the burden. Two northern regions, Veneto and Valle d'Aosta, have declared they will no longer accept new migrants. Others, however, insist Italy must keep its doors open. Indeed, in tougher times, millions of impoverished Italians left their homeland to settle in the Americas and Australia. They, too, like the migrants from Africa and the Middle East, were fleeing grinding poverty and war.
